did_you_know.text: Did you know? Elijah tells Ahab that the dew and rain will cease, emphasizing that it will happen “according to my word”—that is, in accordance with his prophecy.
Did you know? After announcing the drought, the LORD commands Elijah to hide by the Brook Cherith, which is “east of the Jordan.”

Did you know? Elijah is commanded to drink from the brook, and the ravens are commanded to bring him food there. The text explicitly states that they brought him bread and meat in the morning and in the evening.
Did you know? Elijah’s place of refuge is also affected by the drought: after some time, the brook dries up because no rain has fallen in the land.
Did you know? The LORD sends Elijah to Zarephath, a town that the text identifies as belonging to the region of Sidon, and tells him that a widow there will provide for him.
Did you know? The widow of Zarephath describes a situation of extreme shortage: she has only a little flour and a little oil left, and plans to prepare the last meal for herself and her son.
Did you know? The promise of the miracle extends until the return of the rain: the jar of flour will not be used up, and the jug of oil will not run dry, until the LORD sends rain on the land.
Did you know? After the widow does as Elijah says, the flour and oil do not run out. The text presents this as the fulfillment of the word of the LORD spoken through Elijah.
Did you know? In his prayer for the widow’s son, Elijah explicitly asks that the boy’s life return to him. He then stretches himself over the child three times and calls out to the LORD.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the widow concludes from what happened that Elijah is a man of God and that the word of the LORD in his mouth is truth. The chapter thus ends with recognition of the reliability of his prophecy.
